title: Look to tomorrow
hookLine: let every soul look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow (59:18)

lines: WHAT'S WAITING IS WHAT YOU SENT.
cards: Before a long trip, people send things ahead. A box shipped to the new address. A deposit on the apartment.
A message to a friend at the other end: I land Thursday. When they arrive, what's waiting is exactly what they sent. Nothing more.
Near its end, Surah Al-Hashr turns from the story of Medina to a single soul, and asks it to do what a careful traveler does the night before leaving: check what's already been sent on ahead.

teach.b: Verse eighteen. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Observe your duty to Allah. And let every soul look to that which it sendeth on before for the morrow."
The word for tomorrow is ghad, the ordinary word for the day after today. Classical commentators read it here as the Day of Judgment. Why call it tomorrow?
One answer they gave: it's so certain and so near, it's as close as tomorrow.
The verb is qaddamat, what it has sent forward. Deeds are things you ship on before you. The command to be mindful of God, taqwa, comes twice, at the start and after the question, like bookends.
The next verse warns: don't be like those who forgot God, so that God made them forget their own selves. Forgetting God and forgetting yourself are tied together. Hadith give the shipping list.
Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ said when a person dies, their deeds stop, except three: an ongoing charity, knowledge that benefits others, and a righteous child who prays for them.
Three things that keep arriving after you've gone. And a report in Tirmidhi turns the accounting upside down.

teach.h: ALL OF IT REMAINS BUT THE SHOULDER.
teach.b: The family once slaughtered a sheep and gave nearly all of it away. 'A'isha told the Prophet only the shoulder was left. He answered: all of it is left, except its shoulder. What you keep is spent.

how: Muslims often recite 59:18 in Friday sermons as a call to self-reckoning, muhasaba, and many set up ongoing charities, sadaqa jariya, such as wells, schools or copies of the Qur'an, hoping their reward continues after death.

o: the past, everything already behind you
a reward paid out within this life
tomorrow, here read as the Day of Judgment

s: commentators say 'tomorrow' here means the Day of Judgment
they said it's called tomorrow because it's so certain and near.
after death, every one of a person's deeds stops
the hadith names three that continue: ongoing charity, useful knowledge, a righteous child's prayer.
the command to be mindful of God appears once in the verse
it comes twice, at the start and after the question.

games.q: the family has given away a whole sheep except the shoulder. 'A'isha says only the shoulder is left. what does the Prophet answer?
o: all of it remains, except its shoulder.
games.why: what was given away is what remains; what you keep is what's used up.

practice: Picture yourself a year from now, looking back on today: what would that person thank you for? A kindness that outlasts the day, a small amount given, something learned and passed on, a call to a parent.
Choose one, and ask quietly: what have I sent ahead?

wordCard.voice: Ghad: tomorrow, the ordinary word Surah Al-Hashr uses for the Day every soul is asked to look toward. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: what it has sent ahead for tomorrow. ghad is the everyday word for tomorrow.

carryVoice: Your line: what have I sent ahead? Tomorrow is nearer than it looks. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: O ye who believe! Observe your duty to Allah. And let every soul look to that which it sendeth on before for the morrow.
